cases.comparison_subject: A nonwoven sheet formed from dispersed plant fibres is a distinct material architecture from papyrus pith strips and woven fabric, whether or not these materials served similar writing purposes.

candidate_evidence.locator: Printed p.6 Table I: written Xuanquan hemp paper.
2010 abstract: Han fibre paper and mould-formed samples.

comparators.configuration: Ancient Egyptian papyrus writing sheets made of perpendicular pith-strip layers
comparators.contrast: Papyrus consists of two oriented pith-strip layers; fibre paper forms a nonwoven sheet from separated material. No quality ranking or ancestry is implied.

comparators.configuration: Earlier beaten inner-bark sheet; Dingmo stone interpreted as a barkcloth beater

evidence.locator: Abstract: Dingmo implement and contextual 7898 ± 34 BP figure.
Table 1: 7052 ± 31 uncalibrated radiocarbon BP; 7898 ± 34 calibrated BP for sample XA7222.
Material description: beaten inner bark compared with formed paper.

comparators.contrast: Barkcloth is produced by beating an intact inner-bark layer; the paper class is formed from dispersed fibres. Dingmo is an interpretation of a stone tool and its dated layer, not a surviving barkcloth sample, and no lineage is inferred.

cases.limits: The particular writer and date are not known. The Western Han assignment and paper identity follow published, contested interpretations including Pan’s identification of the written material as hemp; the writing fragments are not individually matched here to the separate fibre-study sample. Other early finds, including Fangmatan and Baqiao, have disputed dates or material identifications. The Met’s October 2000 chronology gives an approximately 109 CE earliest surviving written hemp-paper claim rather than the earlier Xuanquan attribution, without directly examining those specimens in its account. The latest bound is the contextual end of the Western Han, not a demonstrated first use, invention or universal availability.
